id: ‘One morn I left him in his bed’

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

One morn I left him in his bed; A moment after some one said, ‘Your child is dying – he is dead.’ We made him ready for his rest, Flowers in his hair, and on his breast His little hands together prest. We sailed by night across the sea; So, floating from the world were we, Apart from sympathy, we Three. The wild sea moaned, the black clouds spread Moving shadows on its bed, But one of us lay midship dead. I saw his coffin sliding down The yellow sand in yonder town, Where I put on my sorrow’s crown. And we returned; in this drear place Never to see him face to face, I thrust aside the living race. Mothers, who mourn with me today, Oh, understand me, when I say, I cannot weep, I cannot pray; I gaze upon a hidden store, His books, his toys, the clothes he wore, And cry, ‘Once more, to me, once more!’ Then take, from me, this simple verse, That you may know what I rehearse— A grief – your and my Universe!

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker’s child dies suddenly after being left in bed one morning.
- The child is prepared for burial with flowers, folded hands, and a coffin.
- The grieving family sails across a dark, moaning sea with the child’s body.
- After burying the child in a distant town, the speaker returns home and withdraws from others.
- Unable to weep or pray, the speaker clings to the child’s belongings and expresses a grief shared by all mourning mothers.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem portrays a mother’s grief after her child’s sudden death, tracing his burial and her return home through stark images of the sea, coffin, and his belongings. Her inability to weep or pray reveals bereavement as an isolating yet universal sorrow shared by mourning mothers.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: One, Your, Flowers

outputs.L1:
One morn, I left him in his bed;  
A moment later, someone said,  
“Your child is dying—he is dead.”

We made him ready for his rest,  
With flowers in his hair and, on his breast,  
His little hands together pressed.

We sailed by night across the sea;  
Thus, drifting from the world, were we—  
Apart from sympathy, we three.

The wild sea moaned; black clouds outspread  
Their moving shadows on its bed,  
While one of us lay midship, dead.

I saw his coffin sliding down  
The yellow sands of yonder town,  
Where I put on my sorrow’s crown.

And we returned; in this drear place,  
Never to see him face to face,  
I thrust aside the living race.

Mothers who mourn with me today,  
Oh, understand me when I say:  
I cannot weep; I cannot pray.

I gaze upon a hidden store—  
His books, his toys, the clothes he wore—  
And cry, “Once more—to me, once more!”

Then take from me this simple verse,  
That you may know what I rehearse:  
A grief—your universe and mine!
outputs.L2:
At daybreak, I left him lying in bed.  
Soon afterward, a voice told me  
that my child was fading—then that he was gone.

We prepared him for burial,  
placing blossoms in his hair  
and folding his small hands across his chest.

Through the darkness, the three of us crossed the sea,  
drifting beyond the ordinary world,  
cut off from everyone’s comfort and compassion.

The fierce water groaned beneath spreading storm clouds,  
whose shadows moved across the waves,  
while our child lay lifeless in the middle of the ship.

In a distant town, I watched his coffin  
descend along the golden sand,  
and there I took upon myself the burden of mourning.

When we came back to this desolate place,  
knowing I would never look into his face again,  
I withdrew from all who remained alive.

Mothers who share such sorrow, understand this:  
I am unable to shed tears,  
and no prayer will come from me.

Instead, I stare at the treasured things kept out of sight—  
the books he read, his playthings, and the garments he wore—  
and plead for him to be returned to me once more.

Accept these plain lines from my hand,  
so that you may recognize the sorrow I describe:  
a grief that fills the whole world for you and for me.
outputs.L3:
The speaker recalls the sudden death of her child, who was left in bed one morning and never woke again. The child’s body is tenderly prepared for burial: flowers are arranged around it, the small hands are folded, and the body is placed in a coffin.

The grieving family then carries the child across a dark and restless sea. As they sail, the moaning of the water seems to echo their sorrow. In a distant town, they bury the child and are forced to leave the body behind. When the speaker returns home, she retreats from other people and isolates herself in her grief.

Overwhelmed by the loss, she finds herself unable either to weep or to pray. Instead, she holds tightly to the child’s clothes and other belongings, seeking comfort in the few physical reminders that remain. Her lament ultimately reaches beyond her own experience, giving voice to the profound and enduring sorrow shared by mothers everywhere who have lost a child.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a mother struggling to comprehend the sudden death of her child. Her grief is traced through the practical rituals that follow his loss: the recovery of his body, the funeral, the lowering of the coffin, and her lonely return to a home still filled with reminders of him. Stark images of the sea and the grave emphasize both the violence of the death and its finality. The coffin becomes a painful symbol of separation, enclosing the child beyond his mother’s reach.

When she returns home, ordinary objects take on a new and unbearable significance. His clothes and other belongings preserve the memory of his presence while simultaneously confirming his absence. These familiar things seem to offer a connection to him, yet they cannot provide comfort. Instead, they intensify the silence of the house and show how grief transforms everyday life: objects that once appeared insignificant now carry the full weight of loss.

The mother’s response is marked not by dramatic expression but by emotional paralysis. She cannot weep, and she cannot pray. Her inability to perform these expected acts of mourning suggests that her sorrow is too deep to be released through tears or contained by religious language. Faith, words, and ritual all seem inadequate in the face of her child’s death. This numbness makes her grief profoundly isolating, as though she has been cut off not only from her son but also from the ordinary sources of human consolation.

Yet the poem also expands her private suffering into something universal. Her grief connects her with other mothers who have lost their children, suggesting a silent community created by bereavement. Although each mother experiences loss alone, the pain itself is shared across different lives and circumstances. Through restrained language and stark imagery, the poem portrays mourning as both intensely personal and universally recognizable: a sorrow that isolates the individual while binding her to countless others who have endured the same devastating absence.
outputs.L5:
**One of Your Flowers**

I found one of your flowers  
pressed inside an old book,  
its color softened by time,  
its petals thin as memory.

You gave it to me on a quiet afternoon  
when neither of us knew  
how quickly seasons could change.

Now, whenever I hold it,  
the years disappear—  
and for one small moment,  
your flowers bloom again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Victorian-style elegiac poem from the perspective of a mother grieving the death and sea burial of her child.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Little Sailor’s Grave**

They bore thee where the black ships lie,  
Beneath a mourning bell,  
While twilight stooped along the sky,  
To breathe her last farewell.  
No churchyard yew, no marble stone,  
Shall mark thy dreamless bed;  
The deep hath claimed thee for her own,  
And folds thee with the dead.

I kissed thy brow, so strangely cold,  
And smoothed thy silken hair;  
Thy little hands I could not hold—  
They lay like lilies there.  
O lips that called me once by name,  
O eyes, my morning’s light!  
The wave received thy tender frame,  
And hid thee from my sight.

Down, down beneath the sobbing foam,  
They gave my child to rest;  
The ocean made thy narrow home,  
The shells adorn thy breast.  
No mother’s hymn shall reach thee now,  
No candle near thee burn;  
Yet moonbeams kiss the waters’ brow,  
And tides for ever mourn.

I pace the strand when winds are low,  
And hear, amid their sighs,  
The cradle-song of long ago  
Return beneath the skies.  
I seem to see thy garments white  
Beyond the farthest wave,  
And call thee through the falling night—  
But none may answer save

The lonely gull, the grieving spray,  
The bell from some dim mast;  
And all my heart is borne away  
To chambers of the past.  
Still, if there be a gentler shore  
Where storm and sorrow cease,  
Thou waitest there for me once more,  
With little hands of peace.

Till then, sleep deep, my only dear,  
Where mortal feet ne’er tread;  
The sea shall keep thee pure from fear,  
The stars watch overhead.  
And I shall love the restless main,  
Though cruel was her part;  
For what she holds I clasp again—  
For ever—in my heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhyming narrative poem about parents carrying their dead child across the sea, burying him in a distant town, and returning home overwhelmed by grief.
counterfactuals.output:
They wrapped their child in linen white  
Before the early gulls took flight,  
And bore him where the harbor lay  
Beneath the dawn’s unfeeling gray.  

The father held him to his breast;  
The mother smoothed his hair to rest.  
No cradle-song, no whispered plea  
Could wake him on the waking sea.  

The sails were raised, the ropes were drawn;  
Their homeland faded with the dawn.  
The waves, like mourners dressed in foam,  
Kept asking why they left their home.  

All day they crossed the bitter blue,  
While cold and salt around them blew.  
All night the stars, remote and mild,  
Looked down upon their silent child.  

At last, beyond a foreign bay,  
A town of weathered houses lay.  
Its bells were slow, its steeples brown,  
And strangers led them through the town.  

They dug beneath a cypress tree,  
On soil that faced the distant sea.  
The mother laid one final flower;  
The father stood as still as tower.  

“Sleep here,” they said, “though far from where  
You learned our names and breathed our air.  
Though strange the earth and strange the sky,  
Our love will keep you always nigh.”  

They turned away when day was done,  
Two shadows lengthened into one.  
Behind them, under evening’s dome,  
Their child remained; they journeyed home.  

The sea that bore three out that day  
Brought only two the homeward way.  
Each wave struck hard against the side,  
As if the whole wide ocean cried.  

They reached their door at morning’s chill  
And found his little chamber still:  
The wooden horse, the folded clothes,  
The cup, the book, the faded rose.  

Then grief, so long held mute and deep,  
Rose like the sea and would not sleep.  
They wept until the light was dim,  
For home was full—and void—of him.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a sorrowful poem in archaic language that begins with a child dying in bed and ends by describing grief as a universal experience.
counterfactuals.output:
Upon his little bed the child lay dying,  
Whilst waning tapers trembled in the gloom;  
His mother knelt, her prayer to Heaven crying,  
Yet Death stood silent in the narrow room.  

“Abide with me,” quoth she, “O heart most dear;  
The dawn shall wake, and thou shalt wake withal.”  
But still he grew, as winter moonlight, clear,  
And faint his breath as snowflakes when they fall.  

Then ceased the bird within his breast to sing;  
His small hand cooled beneath her fruitless kiss.  
No morn could thence its former gladness bring,  
Nor mercy mend the world bereft of his.  

She marked the sun ascend the eastern height,  
And deemed it cruel that day should yet be fair;  
For how could fields endure such golden light,  
Or heaven keep blue, whilst sorrow darkened there?  

Yet every door hath heard the mourner’s tread,  
And every age hath wept beside a bier;  
From crowned king unto the lowliest shed,  
All mortal hearts have harboured grief and fear.  

Thus none beneath the stars doth mourn alone:  
One ancient woe through all our blood is driven;  
For grief is earth’s inheritance and own—  
The common tear of all beneath high Heaven.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a bereaved mother addressing other mourning mothers. Write a bleak, lyrical monologue about her child’s coffin, abandoned toys and clothes, and her inability to weep or pray.
counterfactuals.output:
Mothers, you know the smallness of the coffin.

No carpenter should learn such measurements. No tree should be asked to narrow itself around a child. Yet there it was beneath the winter window: pale wood, brass handles, a white lining soft as the inside of a cradle. They had folded his hands as if he had merely grown tired of reaching for me.

At home, his toys remain where morning left them. A wooden horse lies on its side beneath the table. One red wheel is still turning in my mind. His soldiers stand guard along the sill, brave and useless. The cloth rabbit waits under the bed, one ear bent, keeping faith with the dust.

His clothes are worse.

The little shirts remember the shape of him. The blue coat hangs by the door, holding its sleeves open. His shoes still carry dried mud in their grooves—earth from the last place he walked, before the earth took all of him. I cannot wash them. I cannot move them. I pass through the rooms like a thief afraid to disturb the life that has vanished.

You ask if I have wept.

No. Grief has sealed my eyes with salt. The tears are somewhere deeper, drowned in a country without rivers. People touch my arm and wait for me to break, but I do not break. I endure, which is more terrible. A shattered cup is finished; I remain on the table.

And I cannot pray.

Every prayer turns to ash before it reaches my mouth. What name should I call heaven by, when heaven did not answer his fever? What god requires a mother to close a coffin and then go home to a bed too large, a spoon too small, a silence wearing her child’s face?

Mothers, forgive me. I have no comfort to give you.

Only this: at night I sit among his abandoned things and listen. The house settles. The branches scrape the roof. Somewhere, pipes groan in the walls. And for one merciless instant I think I hear his footstep in the hall.

I rise.

I open the door.

Nothing is there but the dark, waiting to be mistaken for him.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a nineteenth-century-style poem in rhyming tercets about the death of a young boy, his nighttime voyage in a coffin, and his mother’s enduring isolation afterward.
counterfactuals.output:
At vesper-tide the little casement shone,  
But Death had claimed the child beside the stone,  
And left his mother in the dusk alone.  

They laid him where the pale white lilies sleep,  
Within an oaken bark, both still and deep,  
While midnight gathered on the mourning steep.  

No sail was spread, no mortal oar was plied;  
The black stream bore him from the silent side,  
And one wan star went with him for a guide.  

The willows bowed like mourners by the wave,  
The moon made silver all his narrow grave,  
And winds sang low above the gentle brave.  

Through mist he passed, beneath the ruined mill,  
Past fields where once his childish voice rang shrill—  
Now hoof and bell and thrush alike were still.  

His mother watched until the star grew dim,  
And all the world was but the loss of him;  
The dawn arose, yet left her chamber grim.  

Long years have clothed the churchyard wall with green,  
And strangers dwell where once his face was seen;  
She keeps one candle where his bed hath been.  

And when at night the river murmurs low,  
She hears his coffin through the darkness go—  
Still bound for shores no mother’s tears may know.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
